questions.q: Define situational irony and give one example from "A Pair of Mustachios" where the outcome is the opposite of what a character intends.
questions.a: Situational irony occurs when the actual outcome of a situation is sharply contrary to what was expected or intended. In the story, Khan Azam Khan pawns his ancestral necklace to force Ramanand to lower his moustache tip, but the moment he leaves, Ramanand raises the other tip—so Khan's sacrifice achieves nothing permanent. A wrong answer (e.g., "irony is when something funny happens") reveals confusion between irony and mere humour or coincidence.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how the tiger moustache functions as a symbol in the story. What abstract idea does it represent beyond being a style of facial hair?
questions.a: The tiger moustache symbolizes feudal pride, inherited nobility, and a rigid class identity that Khan Azam Khan clings to despite his poverty. It represents the hollow grandeur of a bygone era—he has no land or wealth, yet the moustache makes him feel superior. A wrong answer (e.g., "it shows he is brave like a tiger") misses the socio-historical symbolism and treats it as a simple character trait.

questions.q: Apply the concept of verbal irony to the dialogue where Ramanand says, "My humble milk-skimmer doesn't look a bit like your valiant tiger moustache." What does he literally say, and what does he actually mean?
questions.a: Literally, Ramanand calls his own moustache a "humble milk-skimmer" (goat style) and denies it resembles the tiger moustache. Actually, he is mocking Khan's obsession because he has just lowered one tip under pressure but keeps the other up, deliberately mimicking the tiger style while pretending innocence. A wrong answer that takes the words at face value shows inability to detect sarcasm and the power dynamic hidden in polite language.

questions.q: Analyze the dramatic irony in the final scene where Ramanand mutters, "My father was a Sultan," after Khan Azam Khan walks away. What does the reader know that Khan does not, and how does this change the meaning of the whole conflict?
questions.a: The reader learns that Ramanand, the "lentil-eating moneylender" with the goat moustache, is actually of royal descent (his father was a Sultan), while Khan Azam Khan, who prides himself on his Afghan nobility, may be descended from sweepers. This reverses the entire class hierarchy the moustaches were meant to enforce: the "goat" is secretly a "lion," and the "tiger" may be a fraud. A wrong answer that ignores this revelation or treats it as a mere joke fails to see how dramatic irony exposes the absurdity of the class system.

questions.q: Evaluate the author's use of the deed (the legal document transferring Khan's goods and chattels) as a symbol. Does it strengthen or weaken the story's critique of feudal pride? Justify your view.
questions.a: The deed strengthens the critique because it transforms Khan's abstract pride into a concrete, legally binding self-destruction: he signs away his last possessions to protect a moustache tip. The document symbolizes how feudal honour has become a commodity that the merchant class can buy and enforce. A weak answer might say "it shows Khan is foolish" without linking the deed to the larger symbolism of the new commercial order replacing the old feudal one.

questions.q: Create a new ending for the story that uses situational irony to reveal a different truth about the moustache symbolism. Write 3-4 sentences.
questions.a: A strong answer might have Khan Azam Khan return years later, penniless but with his tiger moustache perfectly upright, only to find Ramanand's shop replaced by a corporate bank—and the new manager, clean-shaven, asks Khan to sign a digital deed for his moustache rights. This updates the irony: the symbol persists, but the class war has moved beyond moustaches. A poor answer simply repeats the existing ending or adds a moral lesson without irony.
